The literature mentions that instruments of this family could accompany church singing and that they appear in the folk music of Lithuania Minor and Samogitia. In 1895 and 1898 Vincas Kudirka published two collections of folk songs arranged for choir under the title Kanklės. In 1906 Pranas Puskunigis founded an ensemble of kanklės players at Skriaudžiai, its members mostly students of the Viveriai teachers' school. The concert kanklės appeared in 1964, based mostly on the northwest Samogitian and Suvalkija types, and used for concert performance.

The kanklės is a Lithuanian plucked instrument of the Baltic box-zither family, also called the Baltic psaltery, H-S number 314.122-5. The body is hollowed from a single trapezoidal block, covered with a thin soundboard and cut with flower-shaped or star-shaped soundholes; metal or gut strings run parallel to the soundboard, tied at one end to a metal bar at the narrow end and at the other to the tuning pegs. It is usually played resting on the knees, with the fingers or a pick of bone or quill. It is used in Lithuanian folk music, choral singing and ensembles, and it is also taught at the Lithuanian Academy of Music and Theatre.
比魯特·扎拉利內認為，西歐傳入的詩班琴自15世紀可能用於立陶宛教會歌唱伴奏，後進: Birutė Žalalienė holds that the psaltery brought in from western Europe may have accompanied church singing in Lithuania from the fifteenth century, and that it later entered the folk music of Lithuania Minor and Samogitia. In 1580 Jonas Bretkūnas first used the name "kanklės" in his translation of the Bible. In 1895 and 1898 Vincas Kudirka published two collections of choral folk songs, Kanklės. In 1906 Pranas Puskunigis formed a playing ensemble at Skriaudžiai; a school opened at Kaunas in 1930, and from 1945 the instrument entered the Lithuanian Academy of Music and Theatre. In 1964 Kupčiukas built the concert model to the design of Stipulis and Mataitienė, extending the range and adding semitones.
